extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and anyone assessing testimony or empirical claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for judging the credibility of testimony, the improbability of alleged facts (including miracles and coincidences), and the reliability of observation as a basis for induction. Emphasises how to weigh antecedent probabilities, possible counteracting causes, witness motives, and the distinction between sensation and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle evidence requires prior belief or extraordinary antecedent probability
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence can prove a miracle to anyone who did not previously believe the existence of a being or beings with supernatural power; the only antecedent improbability ascribed to a miracle is the improbability that any such cause existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The miracle, as an extraordinary fact, may be certified by senses or testimony, but nothing can ever prove it is a miracle because there is always the alternative hypothesis of some unknown natural cause. Those who already believe in a supernatural being weigh between a supernatural and an unknown natural agency, considering conformity to the supposed agent's character. Given the acknowledged general uniformity of nature, there is a presumption against divine agency not operating through general laws, so an antecedent improbability attends every miracle that must be outweighed by extraordinary antecedent probability from special circumstances of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbelieve assertions that conflict with an ascertained law of causation unless an adequate counteracting cause existed
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion that a cause has been defeated of an effect which is connected with it by a completely ascertained law of causation is to be disbelieved or not according to the probability that there existed in the particular instance an adequate counteracting cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate antecedent improbability by considering the known causes capable of counteracting the given causes and using prior knowledge of their frequency or rarity. You need only judge probability of their having existed at the particular time and place, not in nature generally. Weigh this against the probability of false or mendacious testimony; suspend belief until further sifting if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When alleged facts conflict with mere uniformities of co-existence (kinds), require confirmation unless not incompatible with larger kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts that assert existence of a new Kind are not inherently incredible and are rejected only if the improbability that such a variety would have gone undiscovered is greater than that of error or mendacity in witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions by credible persons about unexplored places are often provisionally accepted but regarded as requiring confirmation from subsequent observers unless the alleged properties contradict known properties of a larger kind (i.e., disjoining properties that have always been found together). If the generalization to be violated is very special and limited, suspend judgment pending inquiry; if the generalization is comprehensive, admit exceptions only upon evidence of causation proved by more complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal laws and very general uniformities admit no credible exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities true of all things (laws of number and extension, and the law of causation itself) are probably the only ones exceptions to which are absolutely and permanently incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions contradicting these very general laws are commonly confined to the term 'impossibility' (total impossibility). Violations of less general laws should be qualified as impossible only 'in the circumstances of the case' or unless some counteracting cause (not present) existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no suspicious circumstances exist, suspend judgment on anomalous testimony until independent confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where testimony does not contradict the highest-order general laws and only implies unknown causes or an anomalous Kind in insufficiently explored circumstances, a cautious person will neither admit nor reject the testimony but will wait for confirmation at other times and from other unconnected sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the appropriate conduct for the judicious inquirer: do not accept anomalies on single or isolated testimony absent corroboration, provided the testimony presents no suspicious circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for causes of unreliable testimony in anomalies (fallacious appearances, epidemic delusion, passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In recorded cases where many witnesses of good reputation testified to what proved untrue, there have almost always been circumstances that would have rendered the testimony untrustworthy on inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for means of accounting for impressions (optical illusions, hallucinations), epidemic delusion propagated by popular feeling, or strong interests implicated—religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, or passion for the marvelous—which commonly explain apparently strong testimony for anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish improbability before the fact from improbability after it
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between improbability of a mere guess being right (before the fact) and the improbability of an alleged fact being true (after it has been asserted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many events are improbable before they occur but are not incredible after being affirmed because they are not contrary to any induction. Examples: a single die-throw is unlikely to be ace beforehand, but if a credible witness asserts ace was thrown, that is not grounds for disbelief. Do not reject facts merely because they were improbable a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness alone is no reason to disbelieve an affirmed fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The improbability or unusualness of any fact is no reason for disbelieving it if the nature of the case renders it certain that something equally unusual must have happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many specific outcomes are individually unlikely but one of them had to occur; hence testimony to a particular unusual occurrence is not necessarily suspect solely because it was a priori improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidences often seem to require stronger evidence because they excite wonder and motives to falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of chances that present peculiar regularity (coincidences) are generally regarded as more improbable and as requiring much stronger evidence to render them credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disposition is grounded in memory limitations and in motives: coincidences excite wonder and the desire to astonish, increasing chances of falsehood. But some witnesses, if extraordinary occurrences would make them more careful, could make the reverse true. Each instance must be judged on its particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether a coincidence is better explained by chance or by design (comparative cause-likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular series (e.g., repeatedly throwing sixes) are not less likely than irregular series to occur by chance, but they are much more likely to be produced by design (a constant cause), so when known to have happened we compare probabilities of alternative causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to comparative likelihoods of causes: if a constant cause (e.g., unfair dice) would very likely produce the observed regularity whereas chance would not, attribute the effect to that cause. Use results like Laplace’s theorem to weigh increased probability of design after few repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace’s 'black/white ball' caution—credibility depends on structure of possible errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace argued that testimony asserting a rare outcome (white ball) is less credible because false announcements concentrate on that outcome; but this depends on assumptions about how witness errors distribute among alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept Laplace’s general conclusion uncritically: if the witness has only one form of error to guard against, or if the alternatives are not psychologically or practically symmetric, the argument fails. Credibility must be assessed with attention to what errors or biases are realistically available to the witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the distribution and nature of possible errors when judging testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness is less likely to mistake when there is only one form of error to guard against than when there are many different possible errors; whether errors concentrate on a particular announced outcome depends on how the alternatives are perceived by the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the alternatives are distinguishable to the witness, whether their interests or mistakes could bias toward particular outcomes, whether numbers/naming create many distinct errors vs only two categories, and whether context creates asymmetry in likely misstatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and prior testing of the instrument or source affect credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have previously tried the dice (or otherwise tested the source) and know by ample experience that they were fair, subsequent extraordinary claims about them require different evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior direct verification of the conditions or apparatus changes the comparative probabilities—evidence from someone asserting an extraordinary event in absence of such prior checks must be weighed differently than assertions about an event observed under known reliable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: To rely on observation, ensure the claim is direct observation not inference from sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole condition for relying on observation is that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; observation extends only to sensations, not the inferences drawn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize whether the asserted fact is a direct perception (sensation) or an inference (e.g., 'I heard a man's voice' involves inferring a man's voice from a sound). Many 'errors of sense' are really erroneous inferences from genuine sensations; separate sensations from inferred causes when assessing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that errors of sense are errors of inference; check for hallucination, disguise, or similar appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: What are vulgarly called errors of sense are not errors of sense but erroneous inferences from sense; sensations themselves may be genuine while the judgment as to their cause is ill-grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternative explanations—optical deceptions, hallucinations, dreams, states of nervous disorder, or cleverly disguised real circumstances—that could produce the same sensations. Reflection and analysis can reveal when intuitive perceptions are habits of inference rather than direct certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational data used in induction must be evaluated for the conditions that make observations trustworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction depends on observations, but the individual facts from which we generalize are scarcely ever obtained by observation alone; observation provides sensations and inferences are made from those sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using observational facts as premises for induction, inquire under what conditions the observations can be relied on. This is a logical question about estimation of evidence, not an educational question about how to be a good observer—check for circumstances that could have produced deceptive sensations or incorrect inferences.
